Chapter 01 · The Physics

Conservation laws, grids, and the problem of shocks

Before any neural network enters the picture, there is a much older problem: how do you numerically simulate a fluid that can form a shock wave — a genuine mathematical discontinuity — without your simulation either smearing it into mush or blowing up in ugly oscillations?

1.1 · What a conservation law actually says

Sod's shock tube, Burgers' equation, the Euler equations — all of these are conservation laws. In one dimension, the generic form is:

∂t u + ∂x f(u) = 0
u — the conserved quantity (density, momentum, energy…)
f(u) — the flux: how much of u is flowing past a point per unit time

Read it as: the amount of stuff in a tiny region changes only because stuff flows in or out through its edges — nothing is created or destroyed. That's the whole physical content. The three PDEs this project works with are all this same equation with a different f:

  • Linear advection: f(u) = au. A shape just translates at constant speed a, unchanged forever. The simplest possible test — if a scheme can't get this right, nothing else matters.
  • Burgers' equation: f(u) = u²/2. Nonlinear: faster-moving parts of the wave catch up to slower parts ahead of them. A perfectly smooth initial condition can steepen into a genuine shock in finite time — this is the simplest equation that actually creates a discontinuity from smooth data, which is why it's a standard "smooth to shock" benchmark.
  • The Euler equations: a system of three coupled conservation laws (density ρ, momentum ρu, energy E) describing an inviscid compressible gas. This is the real target — Sod's shock tube, Shu–Osher, Lax, and Woodward–Colella are all Euler problems.

1.2 · Finite volumes: you never actually see a point value

A simulation doesn't store the function u(x) at infinitely many points. It divides space into cells and stores one number per cell: the average of u over that cell.

ūi = (1/Δx) ∫cell i u(x) dx

Every timestep, the simulation needs the flux at the interface between two cells — a single point — to know how much conserved quantity crosses that boundary. But all it has is cell averages. Going from "several nearby cell averages" back to "an accurate value right at one interface" is called reconstruction, and it is the single problem WENO and TENO exist to solve.

Why this is hard

If you fit a high-order polynomial through cell averages straddling a genuine discontinuity, the polynomial doesn't just get the jump slightly wrong — it overshoots and rings, the same way a Fourier series overshoots near a jump (the Gibbs phenomenon). A low-order scheme (just use the cell's own value) never overshoots, but it's needlessly inaccurate everywhere the solution actually is smooth. WENO and TENO exist to get high-order accuracy in smooth regions while automatically falling back to something safer near a genuine jump.

Total variation: one number that catches oscillation

To talk about "ringing" precisely, define the total variation of a discretized signal v as the sum of the absolute size of every up-and-down step:

TV(v) = Σi |vi+1 − vi|

A monotone step has the smallest possible TV (exactly the size of the jump). Any oscillation adds extra ups and downs on top of that, so TV strictly increases. A scheme is called TVD (total-variation diminishing) if it guarantees TV never increases over time — a strong, classical guarantee against spurious oscillation. You'll see sod_total_variation and an LTV loss term later in this course; this is exactly the quantity both are about.

1.3 · The test problems, and what makes each one hard

Every benchmark in this project (and in proj.pdf's validation matrix) is chosen to stress a specific failure mode:

ProblemWhat it containsWhat it stresses
Smooth / multifrequency advectionA pure sine wave, or a sum of several, just translatingBaseline accuracy — nothing to discard, everything should stay smooth
Step advectionA square wave translatingA genuine standing discontinuity, moving cleanly, no interaction
Burgers, smooth→shockA smooth wave that steepens into a shock as it evolvesShock formation, not just a pre-existing one
Sod's shock tubeTwo constant gas states, high pressure vs. lowAll three Euler waves at once: rarefaction, contact, shock
Shu–OsherA shock plunging into a sinusoidal density fieldFine post-shock oscillations that must survive — and must not be confused with numerical noise
Lax / Woodward–Colella blast wavesStronger shocks, sometimes several interactingRobustness under much larger jumps

Sod's problem is worth seeing in full, because it's the cleanest illustration of the three canonical wave types a compressible-flow scheme has to handle simultaneously:

Worth remembering

Shu–Osher has no closed-form exact solution — the shock/entropy-wave interaction is too complex. The field-standard workaround (used throughout this project) is to run a very high-resolution reference simulation (e.g. WENO7 at 320+ cells) and treat that as "truth." Keep this in mind whenever you see Shu–Osher error numbers: they're relative to the best available proxy, not a literal exact answer.

Chapter 02 · The Physics

WENO and TENO: two answers to the same question

Both schemes ask the identical question — "given a few nearby cell averages, how do I reconstruct an accurate value at the interface?" — and reach it through several candidate sub-reconstructions. Where they differ is how they decide which candidates to trust, and that difference is the entire subject of this project.

2.1 · The stencil and its three candidates

NN-TENO5 (and classical TENO5 / WENO5) work on a five-point stencil: the cell averages at positions i−2 through i+2, used to reconstruct the value at the right edge of cell i.

In a fully smooth region, an optimal fifth-order reconstruction is just a fixed weighted blend of all three candidates, with weights d = [1/10, 3/5, 3/10]. That blend is only valid when the underlying function is smooth across the whole stencil — if a discontinuity falls inside it, blindly using those weights is exactly what produces Gibbs oscillations.

2.2 · Smoothness indicators: measuring roughness

Both WENO and TENO start from the same ingredient: a smoothness indicator βk per candidate — a nonnegative number built from squared differences of nearby cell values, that stays small where the candidate's stencil is smooth and blows up where it crosses a discontinuity.

β0 = (13/12)(ūi−2 − 2ūi−1 + ūi)² + ¼(ūi−2 − 4ūi−1 + 3ūi)²
(and similarly for β1, β2 on their own three cells — these are the classical Jiang–Shu indicators, used unchanged by TENO)

Below, computed for real using this project's own teno5_smoothness_indicators on a synthetic signal with one smooth region and one sharp transition:

2.3 · WENO: soft, continuous blending

WENO turns βk into a nonlinear weight ωk for each candidate, using the optimal linear weights dk as a starting point and suppressing any candidate whose βk is large:

αk = dk / (ε + βk)²     ωk = αk / Σj αj

Every candidate always contributes something — ωk can get very small near a discontinuity, but it is never forced to exactly zero. This is smooth and fully differentiable everywhere, which matters enormously later in this course.

2.4 · TENO: a hard keep/discard cutoff

TENO takes a different philosophy: normalize a "how much smoother is the smoothest candidate than this one" ratio into a scale-separation value χk ∈ [0, 1], then threshold it — a candidate is either fully kept or fully discarded, with no in-between:

τ5 = |β0 − β2|     ηk = τ5 / (βk + ε)     keepk = [χk ≥ cutoff]
χk is a softmax-normalized version of (C + ηk)power — the exact formula this project's teno5_selection_values implements. Note ηk here is exactly the ηk ratio proj.pdf proposes exposing directly as a network input in its Step 1 — it's already an intermediate quantity inside TENO5's own formula, just never previously handed to the classifier explicitly.

Kept candidates get re-blended with the same linear weights dk, renormalized over whichever survived; if every candidate is discarded, TENO falls back to the plain cell value (first order, but never oscillates). This ENO-style all-or-nothing decision is precisely what NN-TENO5's classifier is trained to imitate or replace — a network with three sigmoid outputs, one per candidate, each predicting "troubled (discard)" vs. "smooth (keep)."

The one distinction to hold onto

WENO degrades gracefully and continuously. TENO makes a hard yes/no call per candidate. Both use the exact same underlying roughness measurement (βk); they just act on it completely differently. Every idea in the rest of this course — the network architecture, why a differentiable loss is hard to build, the entire premise of proj.pdf — traces back to this one fork.

2.5 · Two more physics ingredients you'll see reused

CFL condition & time stepping. A simulation can't take an arbitrarily large timestep — information can only travel a fraction of one cell width per step, controlled by the CFL number (this project uses 0.35–0.4). Each step is then usually advanced with a multi-stage Runge–Kutta method; this project (and proj.pdf's Step 3) uses SSPRK3 ("strong stability preserving" third-order RK) — a specific three-stage blend chosen because it doesn't introduce its own oscillations on top of the spatial scheme's.

The Euler equations' extra invariants. For gas dynamics specifically, two physical quantities appear repeatedly as both features and hard constraints: the local Mach number M = |u| / c (velocity relative to the local sound speed — large M means a strong, fast-moving wave) and the requirement that density and pressure stay strictly positive. Losing positivity isn't a small numerical inaccuracy — it means the simulation has produced a physically meaningless state and, in this project's own solver, it raises an error and the run stops (you'll see exactly this in Chapter 6).

Chapter 03 · The Deep Learning

Neural networks, from zero

Everything here is generic deep learning — it would read the same in any ML course. But every term is defined the way you'll actually meet it in this project's code, so nothing here is abstract for long.

3.1 · A neuron is a dot product plus a squash

A single neuron takes a vector of inputs x, multiplies by a learned weight vector w, adds a learned bias b, and passes the result through a fixed nonlinear function called an activation function:

output = φ(w · x + b)

A layer is many neurons run in parallel on the same input. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) — the only architecture this entire project uses — is a stack of layers, each one's output feeding the next one's input. NN-TENO5's network is exactly this: 5 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 3, five hidden layers shrinking down from a 5-number input to a 3-number output.

3.2 · Activation functions: why nonlinearity at all

Stack purely linear layers and the whole network collapses mathematically into one linear function — no amount of depth would let it learn a curve, a threshold, or a discontinuity-detector. The activation function is what gives a network any expressive power beyond straight lines.

3.3 · Classifier vs. regressor: the one architectural fork that matters most here

This project actually contains two different kinds of network, and mixing them up will cause real confusion later, so it's worth being precise now:

  • WENO5-NN / WENO7-NN are regressors. Given a stencil, they output a continuous flux-correction number, trained by minimizing squared error against a numeric target.
  • NN-TENO5 is a classifier. Given a stencil, it outputs three independent probabilities ∈ (0, 1), one per candidate, each trained to answer a yes/no question: "should this candidate be discarded?"

A classifier's loss is binary cross-entropy, not mean squared error:

LBCE = −[y · log(ŷ) + (1−y) · log(1−ŷ)]
y — the true 0/1 label    ŷ — the network's predicted probability
Heavily penalizes a confident, wrong prediction (near 0 or 1 on the wrong side); barely penalizes an honest "I'm not sure" near 0.5.

At inference, a probability becomes a decision by comparing it to a threshold (not always 0.5 — this project calibrates one threshold per candidate on held-out data, to correct for the classes being imbalanced).

3.4 · How training actually updates the weights

Forward pass: run a batch of inputs through the network, compute the loss. Backward pass (backpropagation): the chain rule, applied automatically, computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in the network — i.e. "if I nudge this one weight slightly, does the loss go up or down, and how fast." Gradient descent then nudges every weight a small step in the direction that decreases the loss:

w ← w − α · ∂L/∂w
α — the learning rate. This project uses Adam, an optimizer that adapts the effective step size per weight automatically rather than using one fixed α for everything.

One full pass through the entire training set is an epoch. Weights are actually updated after each small batch of samples, not after the whole dataset at once — both because it's far cheaper and because the noisiness of small-batch gradients often helps the optimizer avoid getting stuck.

3.5 · Generalization: why there's a validation set at all

A large enough network can simply memorize its training data — achieving a perfect training loss while learning nothing that transfers to new stencils it hasn't seen (overfitting). The standard defense is to split data three ways:

  • Train (this project: 70%) — what the weights are actually updated against.
  • Validation (15%) — checked after every epoch, never trained on, used only to decide when to stop.
  • Test (15%) — touched exactly once, at the very end, to report an honest final number.

Early stopping: keep the checkpoint from whichever epoch had the best validation loss, and stop once validation loss hasn't improved for a set number of epochs (patience) — even if training loss is still falling. That gap between "training loss keeps improving" and "validation loss stopped improving" is overfitting, caught in the act:

3.6 · Normalization: why the network never sees raw physical units

Raw cell-average values can span wildly different ranges depending on the problem (density near 0.1–1.0, pressure near 0.1–1.0, but a different PDE's variables could be anywhere). Feeding a network wildly different scales makes training unstable and the learned weights problem-specific. This project normalizes each stencil independently, per sample:

ūs = (ū − min(ū)) / (max(ū) − min(ū) + εnorm)

This is exactly equation (1) in proj.pdf, and it's already implemented in this project as normalize_teno_stencils. The nice side effect: this normalization is invariant to shifting or positively rescaling the input, which mirrors TENO's own selection rule (χk doesn't care about the stencil's absolute scale either) — the network's inputs and the classical scheme's decision rule see the "same" information, just represented differently.

Chapter 04 · This Project

NN-TENO5, piece by piece

With Chapters 1–3 in hand, the actual codebase you're working in should now read as a sequence of small, individually-obvious decisions rather than a black box.

4.1 · The full pipeline, end to end

4.2 · Two ways to grade the network, and why they used to be the same question

Until recently, this project graded NN-TENO5 by teacher fidelity: does its error against a reference solution stay within 1.02× of TENO5's own error? That's a "didn't get meaningfully worse" bar, not a "beats it" bar — and it's a fundamentally different question from does NN-TENO5 actually get closer to the real solution than TENO5 does, which is what actually matters and what this course exists to help you push toward.

Why they aren't the same question

NN-TENO5's training loss is cross-entropy against TENO5's own labels. Even a perfect classifier, with zero training error, would only ever exactly reproduce TENO5 — there is no mechanism by which imitating a teacher makes you better than the teacher. Any measured "win" against TENO5 under this training scheme is necessarily noise: the model occasionally disagreeing with TENO5's own decision and getting lucky, not anything it was trained toward.

4.3 · What was actually tried, in plain language

This project's own experiment log (Results.md) is long and technical. Here's the same story with the jargon stripped out, because every step of it is directly relevant to proj.pdf's plan:

What was triedWhat actually happened
Train NN-TENO5 to imitate TENO5's own decisionsWorks well — near-perfect imitation, passes every fidelity check. But by construction, can never beat the teacher.
Build a stricter check: does NN-TENO5's error against the real solution actually beat TENO5's?5 of 6 benchmarks "win," but 3 are exact ties and the 2 real wins are ~1% margins — consistent with noise, not a trained advantage.
Build new training labels from the true answer instead of TENO5's decision (an "oracle")The labels themselves turned out fine, but training on them unmixed crashed the Sod simulation outright and made step_advection's error explode to 5.3×109.
Blend the oracle labels with TENO5's own, using an "anchor" penalty to limit how far training can driftFixed the crashes completely. But no blend strength ever matched, let alone beat, simply using the untouched original model.

Chapter 6 walks through the last two rows in full technical detail, with the real numbers and real plots — they are the single most important thing to understand before reading proj.pdf with a critical eye, because proj.pdf's Step 2 and Step 3 propose doing versions of exactly this.

Chapter 05 · proj.pdf, Decoded

Your professor's plan, concept by concept

Four steps, each translated into what it actually asks the code to do, with the vocabulary from Chapters 1–3 doing all the explanatory work.

5.1 · Step 1 — a bigger, more physically-informed input vector

Today, NN-TENO5's input is just the five normalized stencil values. proj.pdf proposes handing the network several more numbers it currently has to infer from scratch:

Xj = [ ūs,  c̃WENO/TENO,  η0, η1, η2,  Jj−1/2, Jj+1/2,  Mj,  |ΔP|/P ]
  • ηk ratios — already defined in Chapter 2.4. Handing these to the network directly, instead of making it re-derive an equivalent quantity from five raw numbers, is a genuinely reasonable idea: it's strictly more information, computed for free from data the network already has.
  • Jj±1/2, the interface jumps — |uL − uR|, the size of the disagreement between a left-biased and right-biased reconstruction at an interface. This is a BVD (boundary variation diminishing) idea — a family of schemes that explicitly picks whichever candidate minimizes exactly this jump, on the reasoning that a genuine discontinuity should look like a genuine discontinuity at the interface, not a blurred compromise.
  • Mach number and relative pressure gradient — Euler-specific physical context (Chapter 2.5) that a purely mathematical smoothness indicator can't see: how strong is this wave, physically.

5.2 · Step 2 — where the training data comes from

Two data sources, in a 40/60 split:

  • 40% synthetic — analytic functions with sharp discontinuities, sine waves, smoothed pulses, and Fourier–Chebyshev combinations. This is the same family of approach as this project's own oracle dataset from Chapter 6.2 (built from sine, double-sine, polynomial, step, and kink test functions) — static, non-time-evolving functions where a true local answer is well defined by construction.
  • 60% from real PDE solutions — run a very fine simulation (N ≥ 4096 cells), then project it down onto a much coarser training grid (N ∈ [100, 400]) by cell-averaging, for linear advection, Shu–Osher, Sod, Lax, and Woodward–Colella.
Read before trusting this 60%

This exact idea — exact-solution training targets on a local stencil, for Riemann/shock-oscillation-type problems — is precisely what this project's own Phase 2 already built and tested for the WENO7-NN network, and it failed for a specific, confirmed reason, not bad luck. Chapter 6.2 walks through exactly what went wrong and why the added BVD/Mach features here might (or might not) fix it. Don't build this 60% before reading that section.

5.3 · Step 3 — the "Unrolled Physics Loss"

This is the plan's most ambitious piece, and the one that needs the most unpacking. The idea: instead of training against a static per-stencil target, run the network through several real simulation timesteps and grade it on the simulated outcome.

un+K = RK3NN(K)(un)
Take the current state un, advance it K real timesteps using the network's own reconstruction inside SSPRK3 (Chapter 2.5) each step, and only then compare to the truth.

The total loss combines four terms:

Ltotal = λ1LMSE + λ2LTV + λ3LBVD + λ4LReg

Reading each term

LMSE = (1/N) Σi (uin+K − ui,exactn+K)²
Ordinary mean squared error — but against the state after K real simulation steps, not a single stencil's static target. This is the term that finally points training at "beats the real solution" instead of "imitates TENO5," exactly the gap identified in Chapter 4.2.
LTV = max(0, TV(un+K) − TV(un))
Zero whenever total variation didn't increase; grows only when it did. This max(0, ·) shape is a hinge loss — it doesn't reward TV going down, it only penalizes it going up, i.e. it directly encodes the TVD property from Chapter 1.2 as a training signal, rather than hoping accuracy training produces it as a side effect.
LReg = ‖cNN − cbase‖²2
Squared distance between the network's current weights and a baseline (safe, classical) scheme's own coefficients. If this description sounds familiar, it should — it's the identical mechanism, described the identical way, as the "anchor weight" penalty explored in this project's own Phase 9, which you'll see with real numbers in Chapter 6.3.

5.4 · Step 4 — architecture and the validation matrix

A compact 3-layer, 32-neuron MLP with Swish activations (Chapter 3.2), plus a projection layer — a final fixed transformation enforcing hard consistency constraints on the output (e.g. forcing weights to sum correctly) rather than hoping the network learns that constraint approximately through training alone.

Test caseMain metricTarget
Linear advectionL1 / L2 error, shock widthEliminate under-damping; TV ≤ const
Burgers 1DError spectrum vs. ΔxExact shock-speed conservation
Shu–Osher 1DSpectral peak amplitudeCapture oscillations without high-frequency noise
Sedov / SodPressure/density positivityInvariant-preserving (P > 0, ρ > 0)

Every metric here already exists somewhere in this project's own evaluation code, under different names — positive_density/positive_pressure checks, sod_total_variation, and the beats_teacher comparison from Chapter 4.2 all map directly onto rows of this table.

Chapter 06 · My Interpretation

Where the plan meets this project's own evidence

Everything in this chapter is something I actually ran, checked, or computed against this codebase — not a general opinion about neural PDE solvers. Two real risks, both already tested against this exact project, and the numbers from doing exactly what proj.pdf's Step 3 (in a cheaper form) proposes.

6.1 · Risk 1 — the Unrolled Physics Loss needs something this codebase doesn't have

Step 3's whole premise is that gradients can flow backward from Ltotal, through K real simulation steps, all the way back to the network's weights. That requires every operation in between — flux computation, SSPRK3 stepping, TENO's candidate combination — to be part of one continuous, differentiable computational graph.

I checked this project's actual numerical core directly: src/core/SimulationClasses.py, src/core/TimeSteppingMethods.py, src/core/eulerEquations.py, and src/schemes/teno_common.py are all plain NumPy — np.divide, np.sum, ordinary array operations, no computational graph at all. And the point where the network re-enters each step, NN_TENO5, calls model.predict(…), which runs a forward pass and returns a plain array, completely detached from anything TensorFlow could differentiate through.

What this means in practice

Building Step 3 as written means rewriting the finite-volume solver — flux computation, SSPRK3, TENO's candidate combination — in a genuinely differentiable framework (TensorFlow ops, or a move to JAX/PyTorch). That's a substantial rewrite of the numerical core, not a training-script change. Worth asking your professor directly whether this rewrite is assumed to be part of the deliverable, because as scoped in the PDF it reads like a loss-function detail.

6.2 · Risk 2 — building oracle labels the safe way, and where the 60% real-PDE data gets dangerous

I built exactly the "40% synthetic" half of Step 2's dataset for NN-TENO5: sampled random sine, double-sine, cubic-polynomial, step, and kink test functions, computed exact five-point stencils via closed-form cell averages, and labeled each one with whichever of the 8 possible keep/discard masks actually lands closest to the function's true interface value — an oracle label, in contrast to TENO5's own scale-separation decision.

Result: the oracle disagrees with TENO5's own label on 23.2% of stencils, and where it disagrees, the error reduction is substantial (not noise) — a real, learnable signal. That's a healthy dataset. This part of the plan works.

But the other 60% has a documented failure mode

This project's Phase 2 already built the structurally identical idea for the WENO7-NN network: replace imitation targets with exact-solution targets, but sourced from real Riemann-problem and Shu–Osher-like simulations instead of static test functions — precisely proj.pdf's 60% category. It failed for a specific, confirmed reason: nearly-identical 5-point input stencils (differing by as little as 0.015–0.028 in distance) had true targets differing by 2.3–4.5. The correct answer depended on upstream wave history the local stencil physically cannot see.

Why the synthetic 40% is safe from this and the real-PDE 60% isn't: static test functions have no "history" at all — the whole function is fixed and fully determined by its formula, so a local window really does determine the true local answer. A real, time-evolving simulation does have history: what the flow was doing upstream, minutes (or just several timesteps) ago, can change what the physically correct local reconstruction is right now, even if the immediate five cells look the same as some other, unrelated moment. proj.pdf's added BVD-jump and Mach-number features (Chapter 5.1) give the network slightly more local context, which might narrow this problem — but that's a hypothesis to test carefully on a small slice of the 60% before committing to the whole thing, not something to assume is already solved.

6.3 · What actually happens when you train on this — real numbers

I trained NN-TENO5 on the 40%-style oracle labels directly (no anchor, no blending) and evaluated it exactly like Chapter 4.3's table describes. The result was worse than "didn't improve" — it was a genuine regression: the Sod simulation crashed outright (a non-positive density, Chapter 2.5's invariant, violated at simulation step 6) and step_advection's error exploded to 5.34×109 (TENO5's own error there: 1.33×10−2).

Why: a classifier trained purely for one-shot pointwise accuracy against static functions has no incentive to preserve the stability properties — bounded output, no Gibbs oscillation (Chapter 1.2) — that are the entire point of TENO's cutoff rule in the first place. A choice that's locally more accurate on an isolated test function can still be destabilizing once it's making decisions inside a real, evolving, many-step simulation, where small errors compound. This is exactly the failure mode proj.pdf's LTV term (Chapter 5.3) is designed to prevent — the PDF's instinct here is correct; the missing piece is Chapter 6.1's differentiable solver to actually make LTV trainable.

So I tried the cheapest available substitute: proj.pdf's LReg idea (Chapter 5.3), but implemented without needing a differentiable solver — an anchor weight, warm-started from the known-safe original model, penalizing the weights directly for drifting from that safe starting point while still training toward the oracle labels:

L = LBCE(oracle labels) + anchor_weight · ‖w − worigin‖²2

The plateau at high anchor strength is the important detail: it isn't still converging toward the original model's performance as the anchor gets stronger — it's stuck at a nearby-but-different, and slightly worse, point. Fine-tuning under a strong anchor doesn't reproduce a checkpoint's exact decision boundary; it settles near it, and "near" turned out to be enough to permanently lose Shu–Osher's margin.

6.4 · Synthesis

Put together, the picture is consistent, not contradictory: proj.pdf's instincts (richer features, physics-aware loss terms, an anchor to a safe baseline) are all things this project independently found necessary or already tried in a cheaper form. What the plan is missing is not the ideas — it's an acknowledgment of two costs this project has already paid to learn about directly: building the differentiable solver Step 3 actually needs is a large, separate engineering project on its own, and the 60% real-PDE training data has a specific, previously-documented way to fail that the plan's new features might or might not fix, and that's worth testing in isolation before betting the whole dataset on it.

Chapter 07 · Side by Side

WENO-NN, TENO-NN, and the professor's idea

Three ways of putting a neural network inside a shock-capturing scheme, laid out with the same architecture questions, the same loss-function math, and — where it exists — the same real, measured results.

7.1 · What each network actually is

WENO5-NNNN-TENO5 (this project)Professor's idea
Kind of networkRegressorClassifierClassifier or regressor, unrolled
Input5-point stencil (5 numbers)5-point stencil (5 numbers)9 numbers — stencil + ηk + jumps + Mach + ΔP/P
Output1 flux-correction value3 keep/discard probabilitiesSame as TENO5-style, via a constrained projection layer
Hidden layersarchitecture-specific (paper's original)64→32→16→8, ReLU3×32, Swish
Grading targetA numeric flux valueA 3-bit keep/discard labelThe state after K real simulation steps
Where the target comes fromWENO5's own reconstruction, or an exact solution (Phase 2)TENO5's own decision, or an oracle label (Ch. 6.2)An exact/reference simulation, always

7.2 · Loss functions, side by side

This is the single most consequential difference between the three. Read across, not down — same row, three different answers to the same design question.

WENO5-NN L = (1/N) Σi (fNN(stencili) − ftarget,i)²
Plain MSE regression (Chapter 3.3). One stencil, one number in, one number out, one squared-error term. The simplest possible setup — and, as Chapter 4.2 explained, its accuracy ceiling is set entirely by whatever ftarget actually is.
NN-TENO5 L = Σk=02 −[yk·log(ŷk) + (1−yk)·log(1−ŷk)]   (+ anchor_weight·‖w−worigin‖²2, optional)
Three independent binary cross-entropy terms, one per candidate (Chapter 3.3), each against a discrete 0/1 label. The optional anchor term (Chapter 6.3) is this project's own cheap, gradient-free stand-in for proj.pdf's LReg — same formula, added for the same reason.
Professor's idea L = λ1LMSE(un+K) + λ2max(0, TV(un+K)−TV(un)) + λ3LBVD + λ4‖cNN−cbase‖²2
Four terms, all graded after K real simulation steps (Chapter 5.3), not on one static stencil. Strictly more expressive than either of the other two losses — and, per Chapter 6.1, currently unbuildable in this codebase without a solver rewrite.
The pattern across all three rows

WENO5-NN and NN-TENO5 both grade a network against a single stencil's target, computed once, ahead of time, with no simulation involved in the loss at all. The professor's loss grades a network against a full simulated trajectory. That's strictly more informative when it's achievable — the network is finally judged on the thing that actually matters, not a proxy for it — but it's also the entire reason Chapter 6.1's differentiable-solver requirement exists. There's no version of this loss that avoids needing gradients through real timesteps.

7.3 · What actually happened, in real numbers

Only two of the three columns above have ever been trained and measured against the real solution in this project. Here's every real result gathered so far, side by side:

Read next to Chapter 6.3's anchor-weight sweep, a consistent story emerges across both networks, not just one: a network trained on a static, per-stencil target can find small, genuine, real wins on some benchmarks (WENO5-NN on step_advection; NN-TENO5 on burgers_smooth_to_shock at low anchor strength) — but nothing tried so far wins reliably everywhere at once, and the closest thing to "everywhere" still loses at least one benchmark the untouched classical scheme was already winning.

7.4 · Where the professor's idea would sit, if it existed today

It's worth being precise about what its absence from the chart above does and doesn't mean. It is not evidence the idea is wrong — it has simply never been measured, because it has never been built (Chapter 6.1). What this project's actual experiments do support is a prediction about what building it would need to overcome:

  • Its LMSE term is the first loss in this comparison that grades against the real solution by construction, not by accident — it doesn't inherit WENO5-NN's or NN-TENO5's imitation ceiling (Chapter 4.2) at all.
  • Its LTV term is aimed exactly at the failure mode that broke unmixed oracle training in Chapter 6.3 (the Sod crash, the step_advection blow-up) — if it can be made to train at all, it should be more robust against that specific failure than either the anchor-weight workaround or nothing.
  • Its LReg term is a direct upgrade of the mechanism Chapter 6.3 already showed has a real ceiling (Phase 9: plateaus at 4/6, never reaches the untouched baseline's 5/6) — a genuine gradient on stability, instead of a weight-space proxy for it, might push past that specific plateau. Might; that's the one part of this whole comparison that's a hypothesis, not a measurement.
Chapter 08 · Reference

Glossary

Every term used in this course and in proj.pdf, alphabetical, for quick lookup while reading either document.

Adam
The optimizer this project uses for gradient descent (Chapter 3.4) — adapts the effective step size per weight automatically, instead of one fixed learning rate for every weight.
Anchor weight / LReg
A penalty term added to a loss, proportional to how far the network's weights have drifted from a known-safe starting checkpoint. Prevents fine-tuning from wandering somewhere unstable. Same idea in proj.pdf's Step 3 and this project's Phase 9 (Chapter 6.3).
Backpropagation
The algorithm (an application of the chain rule) that computes how the loss would change for a small nudge to every weight in the network, all in one backward pass. What makes gradient descent (below) computable at all for a network with thousands of weights.
Batch / epoch
A batch is a small group of training samples processed together before one weight update. An epoch is one full pass through the entire training set (many batches).
Beats-teacher criterion
This project's stricter evaluation rule (Chapter 4.2): NN-TENO5's error against the real/reference solution must be ≤ TENO5's own error against that same reference — no margin, unlike the older 1.02× "teacher fidelity" check.
BCE (binary cross-entropy)
The loss function for a yes/no classifier (Chapter 3.3). Heavily penalizes a confident, wrong prediction; barely penalizes an honest "unsure."
BVD (boundary variation diminishing)
A family of reconstruction ideas built around minimizing the jump between left- and right-biased reconstructions at a cell interface (Chapter 5.1), on the reasoning that real discontinuities should look sharp there, not blurred.
CFL condition
The timestep-size limit (Chapter 2.5) that keeps information from crossing more than a fraction of one cell per timestep.
Cell average
What a finite-volume simulation actually stores per cell — the average of the true function over that cell's width, not its value at any single point (Chapter 1.2).
Checkpoint
A saved snapshot of a model's weights at one point in training, usually the epoch with the best validation loss (Chapter 3.5).
Classifier vs. regressor
A classifier outputs a probability/decision (NN-TENO5); a regressor outputs a continuous number (WENO5-NN/WENO7-NN). Different output layer, different loss function (Chapter 3.3).
Conservation law
A PDE of the form ∂tu + ∂xf(u) = 0 — the quantity u only changes locally because it flows in or out (Chapter 1.1).
Contact discontinuity
A jump in density alone (velocity and pressure stay continuous) — one of Sod's three wave types (Chapter 1.3), and notably not the shock, even though both are density jumps.
Differentiable
An operation whose output gradient (with respect to its inputs) can be computed automatically. NumPy code and model.predict() are not differentiable in this sense; TensorFlow/PyTorch/JAX ops built with automatic differentiation are (Chapter 6.1).
Early stopping
Halting training once validation loss stops improving for a set number of epochs (patience), even if training loss is still falling (Chapter 3.5).
Epsilon (ε)
A tiny constant added to a denominator purely to avoid dividing by zero when a smoothness indicator is exactly zero. Doesn't change the qualitative behavior; different schemes use very different sizes of ε.
Euler equations
The three coupled conservation laws (density, momentum, energy) describing an inviscid compressible gas — the real target behind Sod, Shu–Osher, Lax, Woodward–Colella (Chapter 1.1).
Flux, f(u)
How much of the conserved quantity is flowing past a given point, per unit time (Chapter 1.1).
Gibbs phenomenon
The overshoot/ringing that appears when a high-order (or truncated Fourier) reconstruction is fit across a genuine discontinuity (Chapter 1.2).
Gradient descent
Repeatedly nudging every weight a small step in the direction that decreases the loss, using the gradient backpropagation computes (Chapter 3.4).
Keep / discard mask
TENO5's per-candidate decision, encoded as 3 binary values — 0 = keep (smooth), 1 = discard (troubled). What NN-TENO5's three sigmoid outputs predict (Chapter 2.4).
Mach number, M
Velocity relative to the local sound speed; large M means a fast, strong wave (Chapter 2.5).
MLP (multilayer perceptron)
A stack of fully-connected layers, each one's output feeding the next's input (Chapter 3.1). The only architecture used anywhere in this project.
MSE (mean squared error)
The loss function for a regressor: the average of (prediction − target)² (Chapter 5.3).
Normalization
Rescaling a stencil's raw values into a consistent range (here, per-sample min-max to [0,1]) before feeding it to a network (Chapter 3.6).
Oracle label
A training label built from the true, correct answer (verified against a known exact function or solution), instead of imitating a classical scheme's own decision (Chapter 6.2).
Overfitting
A network memorizing its training data instead of learning something that generalizes — visible as training loss still falling while validation loss stalls or worsens (Chapter 3.5).
Positivity preservation
The requirement that density and pressure stay strictly positive throughout a simulation (Chapter 2.5) — violating it isn't a small error, it's a physically meaningless state, and this project's own solver raises an error and stops when it happens.
Rarefaction fan
A smooth, continuous expansion wave — one of Sod's three wave types, and the only one that isn't a discontinuity at all (Chapter 1.3).
Reconstruction
Recovering an accurate interface point-value from several nearby cell averages (Chapter 1.2) — the core problem WENO and TENO both solve.
ReLU
max(0, x). The activation function this project's hidden layers currently use (Chapter 3.2).
Riemann problem
An initial condition made of two constant states meeting at a single point (Sod is the canonical example) — has a known exact solution, useful as a benchmark and as a training-data source (with the caveat in Chapter 6.2).
Shock
A genuine discontinuity where density, velocity, and pressure all jump (Chapter 1.3) — contrast with the contact discontinuity, which only jumps in density.
Sigmoid
The activation squashing any real number into (0, 1); used on NN-TENO5's output layer so each output reads as a probability (Chapter 3.2).
Smoothness indicator, βk
A number measuring how rough candidate k's stencil is — small in smooth regions, large near a discontinuity (Chapter 2.2). Shared, unmodified, by classical WENO and TENO.
SSPRK3
"Strong stability preserving" third-order Runge–Kutta — the specific three-stage time-integration scheme this project (and proj.pdf's Step 3) uses to advance a simulation one timestep (Chapter 2.5).
Stencil
The set of nearby cell values a reconstruction is computed from — five points, i−2 through i+2, throughout this project (Chapter 2.1).
Swish
The activation x·σ(x) — smoother than ReLU, proposed by proj.pdf as a replacement (Chapter 3.2).
Teacher fidelity
This project's original, looser evaluation rule: NN-TENO5's error must stay within 1.02× of TENO5's own error. Superseded in this course's framing by the stricter beats-teacher criterion (Chapter 4.2).
TENO (targeted ENO)
A reconstruction scheme using a hard, all-or-nothing keep/discard cutoff per candidate (Chapter 2.4), in contrast to WENO's continuous blend.
Threshold
The probability cutoff (calibrated per candidate on held-out data, not always 0.5) that turns a classifier's continuous output into a discrete decision (Chapter 3.3).
Total variation (TV)
The sum of the absolute size of every step in a discretized signal (Chapter 1.2) — one number that catches spurious oscillation.
TVD (total-variation diminishing)
The property that a scheme's TV never increases over time — a strong classical guarantee against oscillation (Chapter 1.2).
Validation / test set
Data held out from training: validation is checked during training to decide when to stop; test is touched once, at the end, for an honest final number (Chapter 3.5).
WENO (weighted ENO)
A reconstruction scheme that blends all candidates continuously, weighting each by a nonlinear function of its smoothness (Chapter 2.3), never fully discarding any of them.
χk (chi)
TENO's normalized scale-separation value per candidate, compared against a fixed cutoff to decide keep vs. discard (Chapter 2.4).
ηk (eta)
The ratio τ5/(βk+ε) inside TENO's selection formula (Chapter 2.4) — what proj.pdf proposes exposing directly as a network input.
τ5 (tau-5)
The global smoothness measure |β0 − β2| — how differently-smooth the two outermost candidates are (Chapter 2.4).

That's the whole vocabulary. Every equation and every figure in this course traces back to a real file, a real number, or a real experiment in this project — if something here doesn't match what you see in the code, trust the code and treat this as the thing to go update.
